#6480. The Best Air Fryers For Faster, Crispier Cooking (2026)

Buzzy as they’ve become over the past several years, air fryers are really just small ovens with fans built into them, i.e., convection ovens. Their fans to circulate hot air around your food, theoretically to but not all of them are created equal. Our years of testing air fryers (and we’ve used over two dozen in that time) have taught us that there are plenty out there that can give you crispy-enough results—but the very best air fryers churn out not only golden brown french fries and crispy-skinned chicken wings, but tender fillets of salmon and even whole roast chickens at the touch of a button.

Air fryers can take a few forms; the robot-esque basket-style models are probably what come to mind when you think of an air fryer, but there are versatile countertop convection ovens that add bake, broil, toast, and slow-cook options to the air fryer functionality. Some even dehydrate and steam too. And most recently more bowl-style air fryers have started to hit shelves, which swap a slide-in basket for a glass container and top-down, air-frying lid.

The best for all varieties of air fryer needs are below.

New in this update: We tested five models in the growing category of glass air fryers, i.e., those with slide-in glass baskets or glass bowl bases with an air fryer lid. This included new reviews for air fryers from Cuisinart, Chefman, Kisimile, and Magnifique, plus retesting the Ninja Crispi against this new crop of similar products.

Most air fryers fit into one of three categories: oven, basket, or bowl.

A countertop convection oven, or air fryer–toaster oven, combines most of the crisping power of the basket-style air fryers you know and love with the multifunctionality you get from a toaster oven or countertop oven. Generally, the “air frying” function is achieved with a perforated slide-in rack, which usually means lots of cooking surface, but the racks are usually shallow and can require careful tossing or flipping of whatever you’re cooking, depending on the dish. But air fryer ovens, like the Breville Smart Oven Pro with its 13 different cooking modes, can do a lot, making them bona fide do-it-all kitchen appliances.

Basket-style air fryers aren’t as versatile as air fryer ovens, but they’re also less expensive and take up less space. They also tend to deliver better final results on traditional air fryer stuff like crisping up small foods that require shaking (tater tots, french fries, or brussels sprouts), for which a handled basket is far easier to maneuver. Minuses are that they can be hard to clean and limited on square inches inside the basket. They’re also sometimes made of plastic or nonstick coated materials, which may not appeal to some consumers.

Bowl air fryers offer some of the best (and worst) of both worlds and also some unique benefits. Most of these include a heat-resistant glass bowl acting as the basket. Some models operate much like basket air fryers, with the glass container sliding into the base unit, while others opt for a “lid” that sits on top and houses the air frying mechanism. The glass baskets make these very easy to clean (included crisping trays are another story), however their functionality for shaking and pausing to flip foods can be cumbersome. But many come with lids for the glass containers, letting them double as prep and storage containers too.

Capacity: 6 qt.Wattage: 172510 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep WarmColor: WhiteWeight: 11.5 lb.Dimensions: 11.8" x 14.4" x 11.9"Warranty: 2 years

What we love: The 6-Quart Cosori Turboblaze Smart Air Fryer impressed us in every test, producing evenly browned and crispy frozen sweet potato fries, juicy chicken breasts, and perfectly cooked brussels sprouts. It has a straightforward digital interface that allows you to easily set the time and temperature and an impressive array of preset programs (Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep Warm).

A few things set the Turboblaze apart from the competition (including the previous longtime winner of this test, the Instant Vortex Slim). Most notably, it consistently produced the crispiest food of any air fryer we tested in record time. That may have something to do with the fact that there’s more space between the crisper plate (where the food sits) and the bottom of the basket than there is in some of the other top-performing models we’ve tried, which allows for better air circulation.

Another standout feature is its variable fan speeds, which adjust automatically depending on the cooking function. Unlike most air fryers that use this tech behind the scenes, the Turboblaze shows you the fan speed right on the display. Air Fry, for example, is one of four “turbo modes,” running the fan at full blast (speed 5), while Bake uses a gentler speed 3 to avoid disrupting delicate foods. Low-temperature settings like Dehydrate and Proof drop all the way down to speed 1.

The Cosori Turboblaze is also a real value pick. The top performer in its price range (100–150) by a wide margin, it’s powerful, versatile, quiet, lightweight, and easy to clean (the brand says both the nonstick basket and cooking tray are dishwasher-safe, though we recommend hand-washing anything with a nonstick coating).

The model we tested includes smart features, meaning you can control it remotely or use voice commands via the VeSync app. If that’s not your thing, Cosori also sells a non-smart version for about $10 less.

What we’d leave: Our gripes with this model are minor. It’s slightly annoying that you have to press a release button to pull the basket out. And while the greater amount of space between the crisper tray and basket bottom contributes to better airflow (and thus better browning), it means food is more likely to fall through while cooking.

Capacity: 2.1-qt.Wattage: 9004 cooking functions: Air-Fry, Bake, Roast, ReheatColors: Gray, red, white, greenWeight: 4.9 lb.Dimensions: 10.1" x 8.3" x 10.5"Warranty: 2 years

If you’re on a tighter budget, have very little counter space to spare, or are mostly crisping up food just for yourself, consider the Cosori Lite 2.1-Quart Mini Air Fryer.

What we love: This compact air fryer did a beautiful job crisping and browning small servings of frozen tater tots and fries, sliced zucchini, and veggie burger patties (two at a time, max). Depending on where you buy, it will only costs $50–$60 (as of publish time)—not at all bad for a lightweight, quiet, digital air fryer with four easy-to-use presets (air-fry, roast, bake, and reheat). It’s easy to tuck into a cabinet and to clean. Like the Cosori Blaze, the Lite has a nonstick basket. Again, while the manual says the nonstick basket is dishwasher-safe, we always recommend hand-washing anything with a nonstick coating.

What we’d leave: Per its name, it’s quite small—don’t expect to be cooking enough food for more than two people in this thing. It also won’t remind you when it’s time to shake your food, so you’ll need to keep an eye on the timer yourself (luckily, the digital display makes this pretty easy).

If you want an air fryer with maximum versatility and have some counter space to spare, spring for the Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro. Breville makes a few different models (which can be found in the kitchens of many of our editors), but this one is the best combination of performance and value.

What we love: This midrange model has been our top pick for years now because of its versatility, build quality, intuitive design, and consistently strong performance in testing.

In testing, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro delivered reliably great results. It excelled at foods that need to be laid in a flat, even layer across the crisper tray (think veggie burgers or salmon fillets), but also handled frozen fries, tots, and sweet potato fries well. Its interior is roomy enough to fit a quarter sheet pan or 13x9" casserole pan, which means it can effectively double your oven space (or eliminate the need to turn on your full-size oven altogether).

This model is also a favorite among BA staffers and Test Kitchen editors, as well as award-winning cookbook author Nik Sharma, who developed some of BA’s favorite air fryer recipes. “I prefer toaster-oven-style to basket-style air fryers, because they’re easier to use for more common tasks like baking, toasting bread, and roasting more efficiently,” Sharma says.

What we’d leave: As with most oven-style air fryers, it’s harder to toss or shake small foods mid-cook compared to a basket-style machine. We also found that, in general, food benefited from a higher cooking temperature (and often slightly longer cook time) relative to the basket-style winners.

Capacity: .5 cubic feetWattage: 18005 Cooking functions: Toast, Bagel, Broil, Pizza, Bake & Roast5 Air-frying functions: Air-Fry, Fries, Wings, Bacon, Crispy ReheatColor: Stainless steelWeight: 15.8 lb.Dimensions: 15.7" x 16.9" x 10"Warranty: 2 years

If you like the idea of going the air fryer–toaster oven route but (1) don’t have the space for the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro or (2) don’t want to shell out $400 in pursuit of crispiness, here’s some good news: Breville offers the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact, which is essentially a smaller, cheaper version of our top pick.

What we love: As with most Breville products, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact feels thoughtfully designed, with stainless-steel finishes and a solid build. There are fewer niche modes than the Pro—no Dehydrate or Proof—but it does include four air-frying-specific presets in addition to a standard Air Fry setting.

We found using the Compact intuitive (the guide printed on the inside of the oven door helped). We also appreciated the “bit more” button, a feature borrowed from Breville’s toasters that adds a touch of extra cooking time when your fries are looking just a touch underdone.

This model performed comparably to the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro in most of our tests, producing juicy chicken, evenly browned cubes of tofu, and crispy veggies. We still prefer the larger model for its versatility and additional functionality, but this little oven would make a worthy addition to any smaller kitchen.

What we’d leave: While the Compact did well in most tests, it struggled a bit with frozen sweet potato fries. This largely came down to overcrowding due to the smaller capacity: While we tried to fit an entire bag’s worth on a single tray, the unevenness with which the fries browned is a good example of the fact that, unlike a basket fryer, countertop oven-style air fryers are best used to cook things in a single layer.

As mentioned, there’s a guide to oven inserts and placement on the inside of the oven’s door, but this is easy to miss, and these suggestions did not appear in full in the manual. Because of this, one tester accidentally cooked chicken with no tray underneath the wire basket to catch the drippings, which resulted in a smoking-hot mess.

It’s also worth noting that one of the major benefits of opting for an oven-style air fryer tends to be capacity, but the Compact wasn’t able to fit more food than our top basket-style pick.

The Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact (L) is much smaller than the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro (R).

Capacity: 4 qt.Wattage: 16005 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Bake, Broil, Recrisp, Keep Warm, plus custom settingsColors: Black, Toasted Oat, Sage, TahiniWeight: 12.75 lb.Dimensions: 13.75" W x 12.75" D x 11.25" HWarranty: 3 years

New on the market in 2026, Cuisinart’s ClearView series of air fryers truly delivers on its name with the introduction of a glass basket model that also sports a viewing window on the top of the unit (the line also features a larger, 9-qt. non-glass model). Unlike other glass air fryers we tried, this one operates more like the basket-style most people expect when they think of an air fryer.

What we love: The ClearView got high marks across the board in our tests comparing glass air fryers head-to-head, almost always offering up the winning results. The controls are easy to navigate, and the functions are intuitive with beeps to remind you to flip or shake your food when your cook is halfway through. In addition to the usual Air Fry, Bake, and Reheat functions, Cuisinart’s also offers a Keep Warm. Plus, there are two programmable custom presets if you’re cooking the same foods frequently.

The crisper plate is nonstick, coated in PFAS-free ceramic, making it a breeze to clean with a little soap and water (or just throw it in the dishwasher). The glass basket is also dishwasher-safe. The ClearView doesn’t have any kind of mesh or grate covering the heating mechanism. We’ll continue to see how this fares over time, but in the meantime it’s nice not worrying about another greasy, perforated plate to clean. Lastly, the ClearView 4-Quart Glass Basket Air Fryer also comes in four colors—Black, Toasted Oat, Sage, and Tahini—and, as with all countertop appliances, it’s nice to have some kind of choice behind black plastic and stainless steel.

What we’d leave: The cord wrap post noticeably sticks out from the back of the unit. While this is probably great for airflow safety, it adds inches to a machine that’s also tall. And unlike some of the other glass air fryers we tried, Cuisinart’s bowl is oven or microwave safe. Granted, the point of the bowl is to air-fry, but if you’re using to carry your lunch into the office after cooking the night before, reheating is a little trickier.

Capacity: 6.5 qt.Wattage: 17256 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Roast, Bake, Dehydrate, Proof, and ReheatColor: Stainless steelWeight: 14.1 lb.Dimensions: 11.8" x 11.8" x 11.6"Warranty: 5-year limited

We won’t go down the PFAS rabbit hole and get deep into the concept of “nontoxic” cookware right here and now (we've got other articles for that), but given the way the concept has come front and center we know some people want an air fryer with a PFAS-free nonstick basket—and for that, we recommend the Cosori Iconic.

What we love: It has similar features and produces similar results to our top pick, the Cosori TurboBlaze, churning out crispy-skinned salmon and beautifully browned Brussels. Like the TurboBlaze, the Iconic allows you to choose between five different fan speeds, which means it's equally adept at turning delicate kale into crispy chips without blowing them around the basket as it is cooking hefty bone-in chicken breasts to bronzed perfection.

And for those looking to eliminate PFAS from every inch of their kitchen, it has both a PFAS-free ceramic nonstick-coated basket and crisper plate.

What we’d leave: Aesthetically, it may not be for everyone as this stainless-steel air fryer looks a bit spaceship-like. But the real downside is the price, which is practically double that of the TurboBlaze.

In the long run: The Cosori Iconic has seamlessly fit into the life of BA’s head of video, Dan Siegel. The speed is what won him over: “I shave 25% or more off any package-recommended cooking time and achieve perfect browning and crisping on every cook. The nonstick surfaces of both the basket and the included rack are remarkably easy to clean, making this my go-to appliance. My toaster oven probably misses me.” He mostly uses it for his two kids, occasionally scaling up to cook chicken breasts for his family of four, which takes two batches. (“It’s not huge.”) Despite the mirror-like stainless-steel finish, upkeep has been simple: “I haven't had any issues; I really only touch the top and the basket.” And then there’s the look. "It looks grown-up, like an actual appliance and not a big plastic toy without looking industrial. The MacBook of air fryers."

We have spent hours and hours over the past few years researching, testing, and retesting popular air fryers from top-name brands, including Breville, Cuisinart, Ninja, Philips, and Cosori. Here's how we put each appliance to the test:

When evaluating each model, we looked for a few key qualities:

This model from Instant Pot is a great option if a full-size (6-qt. or more) air fryer feels too big for your space or lifestyle, but our winning mini model (2-qt. limit) is too small. There’s a lot to love here, including the intuitive controls and presets, the viewing window and built-in light, and the ceramic nonstick interior coating. In testing, we found it did a decent job crisping everything we threw at it, though its performance didn’t quite match the winning Cosori Turboblaze.

This model from Instant was a previous top pick, and we still think it’s an excellent air fryer. Its design, although compact, offers a significantly larger cooking surface area than comparably sized air fryers thanks to the shape of its basket. In practice, this meant our tester was able to fit an entire extra veggie burger patty (six total) compared to models of a similar size and generally cook more food in each batch without sacrificing any of the airflow that makes air-fried food so crispy.

If a basket-style air fryer is what you’re after and you like the idea of being able to monitor what you’re cooking, the Instant Pot Vortex Plus ClearCook is definitely worth considering. This model performed nearly identically to our old top pick, the Instant Vortex Slim (probably because it’s a very similar build). The major difference—besides the ClearCook’s dimensions—is that it has a cooking window located at the front of its basket, plus a button that switches on an interior light, sort of like a traditional oven. This makes tracking the progress of your tots, fries, or chicken wings possible without removing the basket and disrupting the cooking process. Considering that providing a certain level of brownness is one of the chief concerns in air fryer cooking, this really comes in handy. A few more bonus points for the ClearCook: It adds Dehydrate to its list of functions and can hold temperatures as low as 95°F (the low end of the Vortex Slim’s range is 120°F). The ClearCook also happens to be $30 cheaper than the Slim at full price. On the downside, the square shape of the ClearCook’s basket fits one less veggie burger patty than more elongated baskets. It’s also a bit bulky.

The Typhur Dome 2 is notably spacious compared to other basket-style fryers, with 139.5 square inches of cooking surface that fits a 12" pizza, 20 chicken wings, or 11 large chicken thighs per batch, and a digital panel with 15 presets plus a companion app offering more settings, self-cleaning, and one-touch recipes. We used to recommend the original Typhur Dome as a top pick for extra-large capacity, but after testing the Dome 2, which replaced it, we felt its performance didn’t quite merit a spot on our top picks: When filled to capacity, it took much longer to properly cook and crisp food than most other basket air fryers, and 11 bone-in chicken thighs took upward of 45 minutes to get truly golden, a major red flag given that cutting cooking time is a big reason to choose an air fryer over the oven. That said, the Dome 2 cooks food evenly and does eventually get very crisp, so if you’re feeding a large family and have counter space to spare, it may still be worth the investment.

The Philips almost took a top spot—almost. It’s got a generous capacity, the control panel is easy to navigate, and it performs well with minimal user intervention. In other words, you won’t have to do a lot of shaking or stirring to get crispy fries from the Philips. This model did have a smaller yet heavier basket, and it’s loud and harder to clean due to a bunch of interlocking parts. It’s a good air fryer, but with its higher price tag, we feel like there are better deals on this list.

This newer model from Philips has a lot going for it: sleek touchscreen interface, helpful viewing window, and a whopping 16 settings. It did very well in our testing, producing crispy tots, tofu, and fries, but we preferred the design and the interface of the Cosori and Instant models. If you’re looking for an air fryer with a window feature, we’d recommend going with the Instant ClearCook (slightly cheaper at the time of writing) unless you find this model at a discount.

The Dreo ChefMaker isn't just an air fryer—it's also got probe cooking capabilities and app compatibility that make cooking proteins pretty effortless, and is a personal favorite of senior editor Olivia Tarantino. For the purposes of this article, though, we mainly tested its air frying abilities. We found that while the Dreo performed well, the winning TurboBlaze produced crispier, more evenly-cooked results all while ringing in at a third of the price. That said, if the probe cooking feature intrigues you, this fryer might be worth a try.

Our Place partnered with James Beard Award–winning chef and cookbook author J. Kenji López-Alt on this updated version of the Wonder Oven, which features eight cooking functions, a touchscreen interface, and a roomy three-tier 30-liter capacity. Like all of Our Place's products, this little oven is an aesthete’s dream—but looks aside, it impressed us. It’s incredibly powerful, able to crisp brussels sprouts, tofu, and fries up to twice as fast as the winning Breville. It produced tender salmon with potato-chip-like skin in just seven minutes. Despite its smaller footprint, it’s large enough to fit a quarter-sheet pan, making it a good option if you want to save a few inches of counter space.

All that said, while the Wonder Oven Pro is generally well-designed, a few features were annoying to use. The touchscreen isn’t the most responsive. But the bigger issue we had was with the preheating cycle. Preheating this oven to 400°F took 8–9 minutes from cold, which is already slower than the Breville’s 4–5. But more importantly, the Breville (like most regular ovens) takes less time to preheat when it’s already at temp. The Wonder Oven Pro, on the other hand, seemed to kick off a whole new several-minutes-long preheat cycle even when it had just been heated, only after which the timer would start.

Cuisinart Air Fryer Oven 6-Qt Basket Stainless Steel Air Fryer

The Cuisinart was easy to use, didn’t whirr too loudly, included a nice preheat feature, and was about the same price. We also really liked the viewing window you could use to check the progress of your food. However, its deeper square-shaped basket has less surface area than something like the Instant Vortex Slim’s rectangular one, which limits its capacity.

Ninja SL401 DoubleStack XL 2-Basket Air Fryer

The DoubleStack takes the idea of a dual-basket air fryer to a whole new level—literally. Like the Vortex Slim, the DoubleStack’s design prioritizes using vertical space. It’s skinny with the baskets stacked on top of each other instead of side by side like most other dual models. This makes it narrow and tall instead of wide, but not so tall that you can’t nestle it under your cabinets. Despite its space-saving design, you don’t lose out on actual cooking space. The baskets are big enough to fit a chicken, and the wire racks in each mean you can really maximize how much you’re cooking. (Though you do need to remain mindful of not overloading it with food, otherwise you’ll block the airflow and mess up the whole air-frying process.) You can also program the baskets separately and utilize the machine’s Smart Finish feature—which delays the start of the basket with the shorter cook—to have a whole meal ready at the same time. The one thing we didn’t like was the somewhat confusing interface.

Like the Cuisinart ClearView we recommend above, this glass air fryer operates like a traditional basket air fryer, in fact even more so as it features a front-mounted basket handle with slide-in operation. It’s a sleek-looking machine with a glossy top that illuminates when powered on with all of your touch-surface buttons. And we like that’s is relatively compact at just over 9.5" tall, making it great for in-cabinet storage. In the glass category, it performed nearly as well as the Cuisinart across the board with just a few cases of less even results, but we’re really nitpicking. What we didn’t like was the mesh-style crisping plate, which is tedious to clean and sits awkwardly on some jutting posts inside the basket, (though its design does offer a high and low position for maximizing space or airflow). That mesh is repeated on the underside of the heating element, something we don’t look forward to cleaning after a few dozen oil-evaporating cooking cycles. The internal light is intended to help you see what you’re cooking, but it glows red, which isn’t so helpful when you’re trying to keep an eye on browning.

Of the lid-style glass bowl air fryers we tested, this one was the easiest to maneuver with a fold-away handle that makes removing the top easy for flipping or shaking in the middle of cooking. With fine-tunable controls, it nailed crunchy skin on chicken thighs and crispy brussels sprouts with tender centers. More delicate dishes like salmon didn’t get where we wanted on the first try, and tofu cubes required more time than the recipe allotted to get anywhere near crispy enough. It fell short, as a lot of the glass bowl fryers did, on frozen fries, yielding uneven results and underdone portions when using the settings suggested on the back of the bag. We wish the “flip” alert was more than just a light, and it’s a little odd that the “Dehydrate” setting is listed as a bonus because you have to long-press another button to use it. The attached feet also mean the glass bowl can’t be put in the oven or microwave, but it is dishwasher-safe and comes with a lid. Plus, the whole fryer and basket setup is designed to nest inside itself for storage. And of this style of meal-prep-friendly air fryers, it’s the best version.

This Instant Pot air fryer model is if you need something with a smaller capacity. The rectangular shape of its basket made it easy to fit plenty of food inside. It is sleek and has a short profile, which are nice features too. The Vortex Slim just offered better performance.

This is Ninja's basic basket air fryer. It’s lightweight and simple to use, and it does a nice job crisping up fries. The round shape of its basket, though, makes it less versatile than other models on this list. If you’re trying to cook raw proteins or a tray of vegetables, you give away a lot of space with a round basket.

While the Dash looks cute with its retro silhouette and poppy colors, it just didn’t perform that well. Sweet potato fries came out soggy and greasy. Tofu cubes got crisped on one side but were raw on the other, and the round basket could only fit one veggie burger. The two dials, controlling time and temperature, also prevented us from getting more specific in the cook settings.

Panasonic FlashXpress Air Fryer Toaster Oven

This oven-style air fryer from Panasonic performed well in our testing, but we found it frustrating to use for a few reasons. It has 12 different functions, but they come with very little on the display as to what each of these functions truly means. The Air Fry mode only allowed us to select temperatures between 410℉–445℉, which seemed quite high for certain foods. We also disliked the automatic preheating period that we couldn’t bypass even if the oven was already hot (this was particularly annoying when we just wanted to tack on an extra few minutes after finishing a cooking cycle). If you want to do that, you have to take the extra step of once again pressing the start button after the preheating process in order to start the timed cook cycle.

Like all of DTC darling Our Place’s products, the original Wonder Oven is cute. Unfortunately, it failed to impress us enough to earn a recommendation here. While it did fine at cooking tater tots and french fries, it produced unevenly browned, ultra mushy zucchini and tofu that never quite got the crisp exterior we were looking for. The analog controls are aesthetically pleasing, but make selecting an exact temperature impossible (and knowing when the unit is at temperature impossible too). It did, however, make a shockingly good fillet of crispy-skinned salmon.

Rather than a typical basket system, the Crispi consists of a glass container and a PowerPod that sits on top. The idea is that you can store your food directly in the glass containers, and Crispi sets include as many as three basket sizes (with more available). While most food did get crisp in the Crispi (you’d hope so with a name like that!), it took longer to do so than in a standard basket air fryer, and we found that food cooked somewhat unevenly. We tested this unit twice, the second time head-to-head with other glass air fryers, and our biggest gripe remains that there’s no precise temperature control—instead, you must choose between four preset modes (Max Crisp, Bake, Air Fry, and Recrisp). We thought that lack of precision made this model less versatile, and remembering which mode to use for which temperature number recommended on the bag of frozen fries or other foods wasn’t very user-friendly.

The Typhur Sync has lots of bells and whistles, like a wireless probe thermometer (with a built-in charging port), app compatibility, a PFAS-free basket, and nine total programs (including the three found only in the app). In testing, though, it failed to produce as impressive results as the winning Cosori. The fries browned, but many remained soggy, the salmon skin failed to crisp, and the Brussels sprouts didn’t quite get as golden as we’d have liked. While some of this might be solved by tinkering with time and temperature, at $160, we just didn’t feel this air fryer was worth the splurge.

In its defense, Magnifique’s Glass Air Fryer has some thoughtful features: two sizes of glass baskets (4.5-qt. and 2.5-qt.), each with lids, and a silicone base that’s easy to remove for cleaning and oven or microwave cooking (something Cuisinart and Ninja can’t match). It’s also the only glass air fryer we tested in this round that could possibly hold a small pizza with an 8.5" diameter crisper plate. However, there are more than a few aspects that weren’t as user-friendly. The stainless-steel crisper plate (no nonstick coating whatsoever) was the most difficult to clean by far, not only because of that lack of coating but because of the perforation pattern as well. The instructions specifically say don’t use scouring pads, but a gentle scrub with a plastic pad was the only way we could remove all the residue. There’s no reminder to flip or shake your food halfway through, a pretty standard-issue beep on many other units, and when you do take the lid off, you have to actually hit Start again to keep going, something other fryers do automatically. Results, especially with frozen foods like fries, were uneven, and fine-tuning is near impossible as its interface only allows for four preset cooking modes with no customization. If you’re following a recipe, you’ll have to remember which mode gets to which general temperature range and hope for the best.

What is an air fryer? Is it just a convection oven?

An air fryer is a countertop oven that uses hot air, circulated by a fan, to give foods crisper textures than you can achieve in a regular oven or toaster oven. What makes an air fryer a “fryer” is a built-in convection fan that blows the hot air around the food to crisp it up. It’s the combination of heat and moving air that produces the kind of crispy exterior you’d otherwise get from deep-frying or pan-frying. But unlike a deep fryer, an air fryer requires far less oil to achieve the desired effect—and it doesn’t leave your house smelling like a grease trap for days or weeks. So, technically speaking, yes, air fryers are just small convection ovens, but the most classic form of air fryer isn’t usually oven-shaped, rather more like egg or block with a slide-out basket on the front.

Whether you’re a purist and only consider products that contain baskets to be true air fryers, or you find the term air fryer to be stupid marketing jargon for a convection oven is up to you to decide. For the purposes of this review, we’ve included both toaster ovens that contain convection or “air fryer” settings and basket or bowl air fryers.

What accessories should I buy for my air fryer?

There are a few extras you can buy to optimize your frying experience—things like an olive oil sprayer (so you can crisp without spilling oil on the heating element), parchment paper liners, and an instant read thermometer. For more of our favorite air fryer accessories, head right this way.

Alaina Chou: I’ve been testing air fryers and other small appliances for Bon Appétit and Epicurious since 2023. In that time, I’ve cooked countless batches of salmon, brussels sprouts, and frozen fries in pursuit of an air fryer that delivers on the lofty promise of deep-fryer-level crispiness without the need for a vat of hot oil. And I’ve blown out the power in the Test Kitchen numerous times in the process (sorry, Test Kitchen editors).

#6479. Did The First Quarks and Gluons Experience Brownian Motion? Sometimes.

There are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe. One is to peer into the deepest, darkest regions of space. The other is to study the most dense energetic fluid we can create in particle accelerators. A new study looks at how this fluid can behave.

The fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos. In those earliest moments quarks churned among the sea of strong-force carrier particles, similar to the way dust particles dance in a swirl of atomosphere molecules. Only after the Universe expanded a bit did this fluid solidify into the nuclei we see today. By slamming particles together at near light speeds, we can recreate a bit of that early plasma fluid, but only for the briefest moments of time. So we study the fluid primarily by the particles generated by these collisions. In this new study the team simulated how the fluid behaves when a heavy particle passes through it. In the lab this can be done by slamming a proton into a heavy nucleus.

Particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion. First observed by Robert Brown as the jiggly motion of pollen in water, it occurs when smaller particles collide with a larger particle over time. The barrage of kicks nudges the larger particle around a jiggly random path. The smaller particles also collide with each other in a similar way. On a large scale this creates many of the features of thermodynamics, such as the flow of heat and the ideal gas relation of temperature and pressure.

One of the features of Brownian motion is that the distribution of particle speeds is Gaussian. Most of the particles have speeds close to the average, but there are some particles that are much faster and some that are much slower. The distribution is symmetrical; for every 10 particles moving twice as fast as the average, there should be about 10 moving half as fast. This makes sense because collisions are random.

How the Gaussian particle distribution is shifted for higher-energy collisions. Credit: Du Plessis et al.

Although a dense plasma of charged gluons is very different from a drop of water molecules, they both follow this Gaussian distribution. After all, they are both a sea of randomly colliding molecules. You would expect then that when heavy particles move through the plasma, the result would be Gaussian. All the heavy particles would be slowed down passing through the plasma, but some would slow a bit more and others a bit less because of the random collisions. This new study found that for heavy quarks in a quark-gluon plasma this is only partially true.

At slower speeds the result is precisely what we would expect. Collisions are random, and heavy quarks would have a Gaussian speed distribution. But if the heavy quarks are moving at near-light speed, such as a proton in a particle collider, then the distribution is biased. The quark is much more likely to be kicked in a way that slows it down and much less likely to get a kick that speeds it up. This skews the distribution away from Gaussian.

This means that when we study quark-gluon plasmas in a particle accelerator, we must take this bias into account. Using this result, we can better understand the fluid as a whole, and this could help us understand the connection between the hot dense state of the Big Bang and the Universe we see today.

Du Plessis, Jean F., and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld. "Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm." Physical Review Letters 137.19 (2026): 192302. ↩

Brian Koberlein is an astrophysicist and author of the books Astrophysics Through Computation and Radio Sky: 40 Years of the Very Large Array. You can find more of his work on his website.

#6478. FDA Approves Breakthrough Treatment That Helps Children With Type 1 Diabetes Keep Producing Insulin

For children with type 1 diabetes, managing blood sugar is a lifelong challenge, but a newly approved treatment offers hope of preserving their body’s ability to produce insulin.

For children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, insulin is essential for controlling blood sugar, but it cannot stop the immune system from destroying the cells that produce it. A newly approved treatment offers a way to slow that damage and preserve more of the body’s own insulin production. However, families have only a short window after diagnosis to consider the option.

In June 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded its approval of teplizumab to include children and adolescents ages 8 to 17 with newly diagnosed stage 3 type 1 diabetes. This is the stage when symptoms appear and insulin treatment becomes necessary. The expansion was granted through the FDA’s accelerated approval pathway, based on evidence that the drug helps preserve insulin production. Teplizumab was already approved for people ages 1 and older with stage 2 type 1 diabetes to delay progression to stage 3.

Type 1 diabetes develops when the immune system attacks beta cells in the pancreas, which produce insulin to help the body use energy from food and regulate blood sugar. Some of these cells usually remain when symptoms first appear. Teplizumab targets the immune cells responsible for the damage, potentially extending the “honeymoon” period when patients still produce some insulin themselves.

“Insulin is essential in stage 3 type 1 diabetes, but it doesn’t address the immune process that is destroying the cells that make insulin,” said Kimber Simmons, MD, MS, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine and a physician-scientist at the Barbara Davis Center for Diabetes. “Teplizumab gives us an opportunity to preserve some of the beta cells and insulin-producing capacity that a person still has. The goal is to intervene early enough to make a meaningful difference.”

Evidence supporting the expanded approval came from the PROTECT clinical trial, which involved 328 children and adolescents. After 78 weeks, participants who received teplizumab retained significantly more insulin-producing capacity than those given a placebo. Researchers measured this using C-peptide, a marker of how much insulin the body produces naturally.

Nearly 95% of children treated with teplizumab maintained a clinically meaningful level of their own insulin production, compared with about 79% of those receiving placebo. Separate studies involving people with type 1 diabetes have linked higher C-peptide levels with fewer episodes of severe low blood sugar, reduced insulin requirements, and a lower risk of certain complications, including diabetic eye disease.

The timing of treatment is particularly important. Teplizumab must be started within eight weeks of diagnosis, while participants in PROTECT began treatment within six weeks. Earlier research also suggested that starting treatment sooner may produce stronger responses.

Treatment involves two 12-day courses of daily intravenous infusions, typically six months apart. Potential side effects include rash, headache, nausea, and temporary reductions in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. More serious risks include cytokine release syndrome, an inflammatory reaction, infections, and viral reactivation. Experienced medical teams and careful monitoring are therefore necessary.

Teplizumab does not cure type 1 diabetes or eliminate the need for insulin. Instead, it introduces another way to manage the disease by addressing the underlying immune process.

To help clinicians and families navigate these decisions, Simmons led a national group of clinical trial investigators and pediatric diabetes specialists in developing practical guidance published in Diabetes Care. Supported by Breakthrough T1D, the guidance combines clinical trial evidence with experience in everyday patient care. It covers patient selection, potential benefits and risks, shared decision-making, safety monitoring, and treatment planning.

Simmons, who also practices at Children’s Hospital Colorado, co-authored the published results of both PROTECT and PETITE-T1D, a study examining teplizumab in children younger than 8 with stage 2 type 1 diabetes.

“Once a treatment is approved, the question becomes: How do we actually do this in the clinic?” said Simmons. “The way patients are treated in the real world doesn’t always line up perfectly with a clinical trial protocol. We wanted to give clinicians practical guidance so they can have informed conversations with families and make thoughtful, safe decisions.”

The guidance also addresses a longstanding challenge in medicine: translating research advances into routine care.

“Research shows that, on average, it takes 17 years for landmark medical breakthroughs to become widely adopted in routine clinical practice. Closing that gap is essential to getting the best science to people sooner,” said Breakthrough T1D Senior Vice President of Medical Affairs Anastasia Albanese-O’Neill, Ph.D., APRN, CDCES. “Breakthrough T1D is focused on efforts that will close this gap in a way that is safe and supports shared decision-making between clinicians and families. This new clinical guidance serves as an important tool that will help guide timely care for children with a new stage 3 type 1 diabetes diagnosis. We’re grateful to the leaders who provided their expertise and time to develop it.”

The authors emphasize that teplizumab should be incorporated into existing diabetes care rather than delivered through an entirely separate treatment system.

“We don’t want to create a separate pathway that fragments care,” said Simmons. “This is an opportunity to be thoughtful about how we use a new therapy while keeping the whole patient in view. Our specialty needs to stay focused on providing the best coordinated care we can.”

Reference: “Clinical Guidance for Disease-Modifying Immunotherapy in Children and Adolescents With New-Onset (Stage 3) Type 1 Diabetes” by Kimber M. Simmons, Adriana Weinberg, Emily Breidbart, Carla Demeterco-Berggren, Stephen Gitelman, Kevan C. Herold, Shideh Majidi, Daniel Moore, Amara Ogbonnaya-Whittlesey, Neha Patel, Jennifer L. Sherr, Emily K. Sims, Kupper Wintergerst and Michael J. Haller, 11 November 2026, Diabetes Care. DOI: 10.2337/dci26-0061

#6477. The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week

Eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

This diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

Ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

These days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends

Since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

This quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”

The area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The new online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

There is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent New York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

Clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

While the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most important British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.)

Shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

Bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

For my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy new surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

This vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.)

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

Where to eat in Barcelona, Spain, according to a local gastronomic tour guide

All-inclusive escapes have never looked — or tasted — so good

Today guests expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience.

Where to go to rest, relax, recharge, and eat well while doing it
