#6418. Stanford Scientists Discover 3 Hidden Brain Types in Children With ADHD and Anxiety

Scientists have identified three distinct patterns of brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both, revealing biological differences that traditional diagnoses often overlook.

Brain scans have uncovered three distinct patterns of disrupted brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both conditions. These patterns do not align neatly with conventional diagnoses, suggesting that children with similar symptoms may have different underlying neurological differences. Some patterns were even detectable years before children received a diagnosis.

The findings come from a Stanford Medicine-led study published October 16 in Nature Mental Health. By combining artificial intelligence with thousands of functional MRI (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three brain biotypes associated with different combinations of behavioral, emotional, and attention difficulties.

ADHD and anxiety are among the most common childhood mental health disorders, and their symptoms frequently overlap. Clinicians typically diagnose these conditions using behavioral assessments and symptom checklists, but those categories may not fully capture the neurological differences between children.

“The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses,” said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine and co-senior author of the study.

“We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic,” Zhang said.

The researchers found that children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both could belong to any of the three biotypes. Although particular brain patterns were more common with certain diagnoses, no biotype corresponded exclusively to a single disorder.

The researchers identified three neurological profiles, each associated with a distinctive combination of symptoms:

Each child belonged to just one biotype (each child was in only one biotype), but the three patterns appeared across all conventional diagnostic categories.

The model also identified two underlying dimensions of brain dysfunction: cognitive-behavioral dysfunction and emotion-attention dysfunction. Each involved different networks of brain regions, with the three biotypes reflecting distinct combinations of these disruptions. The findings suggest that differences in how brain circuits communicate may help explain variations in children’s symptoms.

The researchers drew on the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, a long-term investigation of more than 11,000 U.S. children who entered the project at ages 9 or 10.

Their analysis included 3,508 children initially diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both; 693 children who received one or both diagnoses later; and 1,947 children who never received either diagnosis. The researchers also examined brain scans from 224 children with ADHD or anxiety in the separate Healthy Brain Network study to validate their findings.

An AI model examined functional connectivity, which describes how activity in different brain regions is coordinated. By combining these measurements with diagnostic records and cognitive and behavioral assessments, the researchers identified brain connectivity patterns associated with ADHD and anxiety that differed from those seen in children without either diagnosis.

The researchers also detected the biotypes in initial brain scans from children who had not yet been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety but developed one or both conditions later. This suggests that certain patterns of brain connectivity may emerge before symptoms lead to a clinical diagnosis.

“We think this means we may be able to use the biotypes as an early indicator of these conditions,” Zhang said. He identified the early appearance of these patterns as one of the study’s most surprising results.

“It could help us provide more timely intervention for these conditions and slow down or, we hope, even reverse their progression.”

The findings do not establish that brain scans can reliably predict which individual children will develop ADHD or anxiety. Further research is needed to determine whether the biotypes can serve as clinically useful biomarkers for early identification.

Beyond early detection, the researchers hope the findings could eventually help clinicians select treatments based on a child’s underlying brain activity rather than relying entirely on symptoms.

Current treatment decisions often involve considerable trial and error, particularly when medications do not produce the expected improvement.

“When doctors prescribe a new medication, it can take quite a long time, a couple of weeks or months, to see a response,” Zhang said. “If the first medication doesn’t work, they switch to a different one,” a process that can be costly, slow, and frustrating for families.

Zhang does not expect brain biotypes to replace existing diagnostic methods. Instead, he envisions using them alongside conventional assessments to provide a more detailed picture of each child’s condition.

Future clinical trials could investigate whether particular treatments improve the brain connectivity abnormalities associated with each biotype. Researchers could then examine whether these neurological patterns help predict treatment responses.

“We want to find biomarkers that can really inform the right treatment at the right time,” Zhang said.

Reference: “Deep learning of brain–behavior dimensions identifies transdiagnostic biotypes in youth with ADHD and anxiety disorders” by Yong Jiao, Xiaoyu Tong, Gregory A. Fonzo, Ian H. Gotlib, Kilian M. Pohl, Theodore D. Satterthwaite, Jing Jiang and Yu Zhang, 16 October 2026, Nature Mental Health. DOI: 10.1038/s44220-026-00740-3

#6417. Democrats flip the Senate with stunning victories in deep-red terrain

South Carolina Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews delivers her victory speech at her election night party in Charleston on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Democrats won control of the Senate on Tuesday, sending shock waves through Washington on a historic night that saw them flip seats in deep-red states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

Hours after The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats, the party was projected to flip the House as well. As of 1:50 a.m. Wednesday, Senate Democrats had wrested seven seats from Republicans — a stunning result that gives the party new powers to confront President Donald Trump in his final two years in office.

Winning the Senate was considered an unlikely prospect for Democrats at the beginning of the year, given the number of red states they needed to compete in. But strong candidate recruitment and a favorable political environment put the chamber within Democrats' grasp.

With their majority, Democrats are expected to serve as a significant check on Trump, who could now have a more difficult time advancing his nominees through the chamber.

“Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate, and we have five words for the American people: Relief is on the way,” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said Thursday night in Washington.

“The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks,” the New York Democrat added. “As a result, there is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America now and on into the future.”

The Democratic path to the majority ran through several deep-red states that have proved hostile to the party in recent years and that Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

In Texas, state Rep. James Talarico defeated scandal-plagued Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the Lone Star State since 1988. Paxton had defeated Republican incumbent John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.

In perhaps the biggest shocker of the night, South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, a shocking flip in a state that last elected a Democratic senator in 1998. Graham was appointed to the Senate in July after the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, and ran for the full term with Trump’s strong endorsement.

And the longest Senate drought in the country ended Tuesday when Democrat Adam Hamilton, pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist church, unseated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, a state that had not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.

Other flips came in onetime battleground states that had turned decidedly red in recent cycles. In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to complete the unfinished term of Vice President JD Vance. And in Iowa, Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to succeed retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst.

In blue-leaning Maine, a 30-year Senate career came to a close with Republican Sen. Susan Collins losing her bid for a sixth term to Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson.

The night began strongly for the party, with key holds in Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff easily dispatched GOP Rep. Mike Collins, and New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas defeated a comeback bid by former Sen. John E. Sununu.

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper also gave Democrats their first flip of the night, defeating Republican Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman.

Democrats also held the open seat in Minnesota, with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan prevailing over former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya.

A Democratic majority in the Senate could run into a president who has said he would become “Mr. Veto” against any legislation coming out of chambers controlled by the opposition party.

With Trump in that position, Democrats will likely push “for legislation that may set the agenda for the future in case a Democrat’s elected in 2028,” according to Christian Grose, a professor of political science and public policy at the University of Southern California.

But in a Tuesday night interview with CBS News, Trump also said, “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”

With control of the Senate, Democrats are also poised to block Trump’s nominees, escalating the opposition they mounted while in the minority during his first two years back in office.

“Very few of them are going to get through,” Schumer told Semafor in October. “It’s the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.”

Those nominees would likely extend from the Cabinet to the judicial branch, potentially even hindering confirmation of a Supreme Court pick in case of a vacancy.

Schumer told reporters ahead of the October recess: “The bottom line is, one of the reasons we want to do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices — MAGA justices — on the Supreme Court and the lower courts.”

Other Democrats have agreed with that sentiment and pointed to 2016, when Mitch McConnell led the Senate and blocked the confirmation of President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland. That left the seat open for more than a year, with Trump eventually filling the spot with Neil Gorsuch.

As Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters recently: “We’ve got to do exactly what McConnell did to us.”

Senate Democrats will also gain subpoena power, bolstering their ability to investigate Trump and his administration. Those investigations could include his handling of the conflict in Iran, his family’s business ties and wealth gains while in office, or his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

“We have a real duty to investigate all of this just absolutely blatant corruption that’s so dangerous to our national security,” Senate Judiciary member Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said in September, shortly after reporting emerged about wedding after-party celebrations for Trump’s eldest son, which were financed by a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin.

While Democrats in Congress could in theory pursue a third impeachment against the president, the appetite to seal the deal in the Senate would likely fall short, given they would need 67 votes to convict.

John T. Bennett contributed to this report.

The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

Dhungana, S., & Flament, N. (2026). The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity. Nature, 659(8139), 106–112. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

#6414. Billions of trees grow beyond forests – and counting them could change restoration plans

A satellite study counted 5.25 billion trees in Rwanda and Tanzania, finding more than half outside forests, from farmland to towns.

Count a country’s forests and you’ve counted its trees, or so the thinking goes. In Rwanda and Tanzania, most of the trees aren’t in the forests at all.

Researchers counted about 5.25 billion trees across the two countries from 2019 satellite images, and more than half stood on farms, in grassland and shrubland, and in towns.

Countries and organizations have pledged to plant more than a trillion trees worldwide since the Paris climate agreement of 2015.

A pledge needs a count of what is already there, and that count has mostly come from forest surveys that often exclude farmland.

Maurice Mugabowindekwe and Martin Brandt of the University of Copenhagen led the team, with colleagues at the Rwanda Space Agency, the University of Rwanda, and the Tanzania Forest Services Agency.

Their count covers only trees big enough to see from space. That means a crown of at least 32 square feet (3 square meters), or a height of at least 10 feet (3 meters).

The team sorted its count by the land cover map that the European Space Agency’s WorldCover project publishes.

Only 48.8% of the trees fell inside the class that map calls tree cover, which is roughly forest and woodland.

The other 51.2% were spread across everything else: shrubland held 22.1%, grassland 16.4%, and cropland 12%.

The rest, under 1%, stood in towns, wetlands, bare ground and mangroves. Counting only trees in the tree-cover category would leave out more than half the total.

Tanzania accounted for about 5.04 billion of the trees and Rwanda for about 213 million. The typical acre in Tanzania carried 17 trees (42 per hectare) and the typical acre in Rwanda 15 (37 per hectare).

A typical acre of forest carried about 25 (61 per hectare). Forest holds trees more thickly, but there is far more land outside it.

In 2015, a team writing in Nature estimated about 19.9 billion trees in Tanzania, nearly four times this count.

The estimates are not directly comparable: the earlier study included small trees beneath the canopy, while the new study also counted trees outside forests.

Older tree maps worked from pictures sharp enough to outline each crown, taken by drones, aircraft or satellites. Those images cost money, and clouds spoil many.

The Planet satellites the team used have a 10-foot (3-meter) pixel.

The freely available Sentinel-2 optical images and Sentinel-1 radar data have 33-foot (10-meter) pixels.

So the team stopped trying to outline crowns. They stacked 20 bands of data from the three satellite systems into one image and cut it into squares 315 feet (96 meters) on a side.

Then they trained a deep learning model to estimate how many trees each square held, from the patterns of color, texture and radar echo inside it.

The model learned from about 12 million tree crowns in 2,832 sample areas across nine African countries and India. People had marked those crowns by hand or pulled them from laser-scanner height maps.

The team also found that dropping the sharper Planet images and using only the two Sentinel satellites gave nearly the same accuracy.

Rwanda and Tanzania both run national forest inventories, in which crews measure the trees in fixed plots.

The team compared its predictions with 196 of those plots in Rwanda and 19,664 in Tanzania.

It counted only trees at least 8 inches (20 centimeters) thick at chest height, the size most likely to show from above.

The model undercounted in most landscapes. Its raw estimate was about 179 million trees for Rwanda and 3.79 billion for Tanzania.

Matching the field plots raised those figures by about a fifth and a third, respectively, to the 213 million and 5.04 billion reported.

The authors’ explanation is that overlapping crowns in dense forest blur into one signal at a 10-foot pixel.

Built-up areas and mangroves in Tanzania were overcounted instead, and the authors suspect buildings and wetland plants were being read as trees.

Even after correction, the Tanzania figure could be anywhere from 4.6 to 5.6 billion.

A survey of East African farms found an average of 79 trees per acre (195 per hectare).

At that density, the two countries’ 37.6 million acres (15.2 million hectares) of cropland could take about 2.3 billion more trees.

That would be nearly half as many again as the two countries hold now, and trees among crops can raise harvests as well, the authors added.

Tanzania’s own census counts far more cropland than the satellite map does, about 99 million acres (40 million hectares), half of it on smallholder farms.

On that figure, the authors wrote, smallholders alone could add around 3.4 billion trees “if they access adequate support and incentives.”

That is more trees than the count found in all of Tanzania’s forests.

The authors’ point is that a baseline like this one can guide where a government puts its restoration money, and where planting new trees would crowd out naturally open land.

Restoration programs across Africa, from national pledges to the Great Green Wall, have mostly had no such baseline, because operational tree-count systems remain largely unavailable, the authors wrote.

The satellites can’t see under a dense canopy, so the authors treat their own estimates for closed forest with caution.

The count also leaves out every tree too small to show at a 10-foot pixel, so it can’t yet tell whether newly planted seedlings survive.

The correction factors came from Rwandan and Tanzanian field plots, so they may not apply elsewhere.

To use this method elsewhere, researchers would need local field measurements to check and adjust the satellite estimates.

The data and code are publicly available. The team plans to incorporate field measurements into the model to better account for trees hidden beneath the canopy.

The researchers also hope to test the method in other regions and with data from other satellites.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Remote Sensing.

#6413. Scientists Find That Mice, Not Deer, Hold a Major Clue to Lyme Disease Risk

A 35-year study reveals that mice, acorns, and unexpected environmental forces hold surprising clues to predicting Lyme disease risk. A remarkable 35-year study is challenging long-held assumptions about Lyme disease, revealing that mice, acorns, and even extreme weather influence tick populations in unexpected ways. One of the biggest surprises is that deer, often associated with the spread of Lyme disease, may be less important in predicting the numbers of dangerous ticks than researchers once believed.

Diseases transmitted by ticks are becoming increasingly common across the United States. Lyme disease is the most frequently reported, with nearly 500,000 people diagnosed annually. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through bites from infected blacklegged ticks. Antibiotics can successfully treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may spread to the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have investigated the complicated relationships among oak trees, acorns, rodents, predators, ticks, and climate. Their goal has been to understand how these interconnected factors influence the risk of Lyme disease in humans.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences highlights nine particularly unexpected discoveries from this decades-long research effort. Several findings challenge conventional thinking about how tick populations grow and what determines the likelihood of disease transmission.

“On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the unusually extensive dataset has been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from random fluctuations and misleading correlations. Relationships that seem convincing over a few years can look very different when examined across several decades.

“Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare,” said LaDeau. “This research has followed an ecological community — including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms — examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study.”

When scientists first identified Lyme disease in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely factor in the disease’s spread. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying large numbers of adult ticks, suggesting that deer populations might strongly influence how many ticks would emerge in subsequent seasons.

Deer do not directly transmit the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks. However, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks, allowing those ticks to reproduce. Researchers therefore suspected that larger deer populations would support more egg-laying females and ultimately produce more young ticks.

Decades of field observations have complicated that theory. At the Cary Institute’s 2,000-acre forested research site in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant relationship between deer abundance and the number of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks and represent the life stage most likely to transmit Lyme disease to humans.

“We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data,” said Ostfeld, “but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing.”

Although deer numbers did not reliably predict nymph populations, mouse numbers told a different story.

The researchers discovered that years with abundant mice were followed by an approximately 40% increase in nymphal ticks the next year. This relationship makes white-footed mice particularly important to understanding changes in tick populations.

These small rodents provide an excellent food source for blacklegged tick larvae. They are also highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to the young ticks feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can carry the bacteria into their next developmental stage. When they feed again as nymphs, they can transmit the infection to humans.

One of the study’s most striking discoveries involves something seemingly unrelated to human disease: acorns.

Oak trees occasionally produce unusually large quantities of acorns in a synchronized event known as acorn masting. The sudden abundance of food benefits mice, allowing their populations to increase during the following year.

That population boom then provides more feeding opportunities for young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly large acorn harvest can reliably predict increased numbers of nymphal ticks two years later.

This creates a remarkable ecological chain reaction in which events beginning in the forest canopy can influence tick populations years afterward.

The relationship between mice and Lyme disease produced another unexpected finding.

Because mice are so effective at transmitting B. burgdorferi, the scientists initially assumed that years with more mice would also have a higher percentage of infected nymphal ticks. Early observations appeared to support that prediction.

However, the connection gradually disappeared as the research team accumulated more years of data.

“It kept me up at night,” said Ostfeld, “because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.”

Further investigation pointed toward a more complicated explanation involving other animals that provide blood meals for ticks.

When mouse populations increase, populations of other potential hosts, including squirrels, skunks, and opossums, may also rise. Most of these animals are much less effective at transmitting the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks.

Consequently, a greater share of ticks feeding on these alternative hosts can reduce the overall percentage of infected nymphs, even when mice are plentiful.

“So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts,” explained Ostfeld. “It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case.”

The findings demonstrate why predicting the total number of ticks is different from predicting how many of those ticks carry Lyme disease.

Another surprise emerged when the researchers compared laboratory experiments with conditions in the wild.

Previous laboratory studies had suggested that extreme heat and severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that the insects were far more resilient than expected.

The researchers suspect that ticks escape dangerous temperatures by moving deeper into the soil or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less extreme.

However, temperature still appears to influence tick populations in important ways. The team found that years with generally warmer conditions tended to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual.

This creates an intriguing contradiction. Warmer years typically benefit mice, which should help support larger tick populations, yet the researchers have not observed a corresponding overall increase in nymphs.

Understanding how these opposing effects interact remains an important focus of the ongoing research.

Together, the discoveries suggest that Lyme disease risk is shaped by a complicated network of ecological relationships, but one that contains patterns scientists can use to make predictions.

The strong connection between mouse abundance and future tick numbers could help public health officials anticipate periods of elevated risk. Likewise, recognizing that deer abundance is not a reliable predictor of nymph populations at the study site, and that severe winter weather may not substantially reduce tick numbers, could improve disease prevention strategies.

Important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will influence the relationships among ticks, rodents, oak trees, and other wildlife.

“You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far,” said Ostfeld. “We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it’s very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production.”

Since the monitoring program began in 1991, its research site in Dutchess County has undergone numerous environmental changes, including shifting climate conditions, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species.

The scientists intend to continue tracking how ticks and the animals they depend on respond to these changes. By extending an already exceptional research record, they hope to uncover more of the hidden ecological patterns that could help predict Lyme disease risk and protect human health in the years ahead.

Reference: “The ecology of Lyme disease: Long-term data, surprises, and a synthesis” by Richard S. Ostfeld, Shannon L. LaDeau, Kelly Oggenfuss, Charles D. Canham, Michael Fargione, Raymond J. Winchcombe and Felicia Keesing, 17 August 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2610907123

#6412. Trump made midterms about himself, and voters rejected him

President Donald Trump dances to "YMCA" after speaking to a Republican midterms convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas on Sept. 9. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump consistently told voters this midterm campaign to pretend he was on the ballot.

Voters responded by making election night a disaster for the Republican Party the president has spent a decade remaking in his own image. Trump spent his first two years back in the White House focused almost exclusively on his “Make America Great Again” base.

One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, called the election results for Trump a “2006-style massacre,” referring to President George W. Bush’s second midterms when Democrats picked up a combined 37 House and Senate seats amid frustrations with the Iraq war, the economy and other issues at home.

“This is much bigger than a couple of candidates here and there. … The issues were Americans prefer cheap gas and not the Iran conflict, and [Trump’s] tariffs were … an issue given grocery prices,” the GOP strategist said in a text message as midnight approached Tuesday in Washington, D.C. “What’s going on in Texas … could be the shot heard around the world.”

That was a reference to Texas going blue on Trump’s watch, his handpicked GOP Senate nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, losing his race to Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, and Trump-backed GOP Gov. Greg Abbott losing to Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. Trump blamed Abbott, whom he had long praised, in a late-night post, calling the three-term governor a “RINO,” or Republican in name only.

For 21 months, multiple public opinion polls charted the independent voters who pushed him to a second nonconsecutive term in 2024 steadily leaving his coalition. Many of the same polls showed an electorate fed up with the high prices of groceries, health care, travel and other everyday items.

Even as voters already were casting votes Tuesday, Trump continued to dismiss the country’s “affordability” crisis, which he for months dismissed as a Democratic-manufactured lie. The president who long sold himself as the one true messenger of the forgotten American man and woman dismissed voter concerns as a “hoax.”

Down went Senate candidates he rallied for in the homestretch of the campaign, including Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, GOP nominees Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Michael Whatley in North Carolina, and Paxton in Texas.

Several media outlets called Democrats winning control of the House before or just after 10 p.m. Eastern time. In South Carolina, Trump backed Graham over veteran GOP Rep. Ralph Norman, and in Texas, he put his grudge against longtime Sen. John Cornyn — who didn’t endorse him to be the GOP presidential nominee in 2024 — over Paxton’s baggage.

Former GOP Rep. Charlie Dent said “the president's support among Republicans has been slightly diminished leading up to this point, and I suspect it will become more diminished after the election.”

“Over the next two years, many Republicans will be looking forward, not backward, and I think that the president will be less of a factor in the party. He’ll still be a factor, don’t get me wrong, but I think less of one,” Dent said in a telephone interview. “The [2028] presidential nominee, whoever that is, will be the one who will be trying to determine the future of the party.”

An ever-defiant Trump took to social media Tuesday night as the results rolled in and blamed GOP candidates, writing: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Except, he had pleaded with voters for a month to “pretend” he was on the ballot.

One White House official tried to deflect blame away from the boss, writing in an email that “candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.”

But Marc Short, who worked in the Trump 1.0 White House, on Tuesday night said the blame fell squarely on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. “It’s hard to think of a WH that’s sabotaged House and Senate candidates more than this one,” he wrote on X.

Leading up to election night, however, Trump was dug in on defending his second term’s record.

“The inflation is solved. … I mean, everything’s going good,” Trump said Tuesday morning on “Fox & Friends” on Fox News Channel, calling his unpopular tariffs “tremendous.”

“I mean, we have a thing going that nobody has ever seen before, and that includes China and other countries, and they will let you know,” he said.

Trump’s campaign-trail economic message was further complicated by his decision to join Israel in striking Iran. The conflict, which started Feb. 28, defied his pledge of no new prolonged military conflicts, which had been a hallmark of his foreign policy for a decade.

Even as polls showed majorities of Americans placing high gas and diesel prices atop their lists of most-concerning issues, Trump for months shrugged them off, predicting oil prices would plummet, eventually.

“The onus and the blame is going to be right on the president of the United States, which of course he is going to resist,” Dent said. “At his rallies, there were these never-ending comments on things that were just really not connected to what most voters care about, which was inflation and the cost of everything and how challenging their lives are, from a financial standpoint. And the president just didn’t focus on those issues and talked about all these other things that, frankly, were irrelevant.”

Trump would not allow his party’s candidates to put distance between their campaigns and his unpopular second term.

As some House and Senate GOP candidates attempted to run on messages that downplayed Trump, he announced the first-ever Republican midterms convention in Dallas. The primetime spectacle spanned two nights, with Trump as the headlining act on Sept. 9 and Sept. 10 at the American Airlines Center.

During his lengthy appearance on the opening night, Trump got pushback from even some Republican lawmakers when he pledged he would send every U.S. citizen $5,000 — but only if his party retained control of the House and Senate.

On night two, Trump’s loyalists in the large arena — home to the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks — agreed to his demand that they raise their right hands and declare allegiance to him.

The convention made clear Trump would not ease his grip on the GOP.

Then came his October campaign rally blitz, with the president continuing to dismiss voters' economic worries and issue cryptic threats about the accuracy of American elections and what he called Democrats' collective intention to “cheat.”

By the end of his midterm rally sprint, Trump increasingly went for laugh lines, a striking contrast to his fire-and-brimstone events in 2016. Audiences of his supporters from Gastonia, N.C., to Corpus Christi, Texas, to Dalton, Ga., to Salina, Kan., to Wasilla, Alaska, chuckled along at times.

His closing-argument event Monday at the Reflecting Pool that sits between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II memorial on the National Mall offered another example of Trump’s predilection for talking about matters relatively unimportant to voters. He talked about pool liners, his White House ballroom and other non-election issues.

By late Tuesday night, Trump appeared to have moved on, telling The New York Times he would accept the outcomes of the election results.

In other media interviews, the GOP president said he was ready to meet congressional Democrats at the negotiating table but that he had his veto pen ready.

“We’re going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country,” he said on a Politico livestream Tuesday. “They've already called and they want to work with me.”

Niels Lesniewski contributed to this report.

#6411. The 9 Best Multitools for Fixing Things in a Pinch

Cut, tighten, loosen, open, and twist your way through whatever challenges crop up.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For situations where you don’t have your full tool kit by your side, jump into action like a real-life MacGyver using a multitool. These handy pocket-size companions have come a long way from the Swiss Army Knives of yesteryear, boasting major improvements not just in overall design, but in the quality of tools, materials, and the total number of features offered. Modern-day multitools are designed to be twisted, wrenched, and squeezed with just about the same force that any regular item in your toolbox endures.

A good multitool is typically made of all-stainless steel or equally durable metal with as many as 30 tools integrated into the frame. That said, the majority of them still fit comfortably in a pocket and weigh less than a half pound.

There are dozens of multitool manufacturers, so we got our hands on models from established, popular brands like Victorinox, Gerber, Leatherman, SOG, and more to find out which stood out from the pack. Following our tests and in-depth research, these are the multitools we pick up for fixing nearly anything in a pinch.

It’s hard to nail down one aspect of the Arc that I like best, because it does just about everything well. The opening and closing mechanism is responsive and every tool is accessible from the outside. Plus, the 20 listed functions all work well, as opposed to those on some other multitools that feel like afterthoughts for the sake of an eye-popping marketing claim. This effectiveness across the board is precisely why it is our new best overall pick.

In comparison to our former best overall pick, the Victorinox Spirit X, the Arc shines the brightest when looking at its blade. Unlike the Spirit X, which is made entirely of stainless steel, the knife on the Arc is made of MagnaCut. That means it’s more resistant to corrosion and rust and retains its edge longer.

Beyond this, the blade is simply wider, longer, and based on a pretty basic touch test, feels a lot sharper. In my hands, it made it easier to poke through boxes sealed with duct tape and slice off a chunk of an apple.

The Arc also comes with a larger set of scissors, a thicker saw, and a larger file. Furthermore, it’s equipped with a hip clip that slides directly onto your pants while the Spirit X requires a holster that must be looped through your belt to carry it on your person outside of a pocket.

RoverTac’s 12-in-1 initially caught our eye because it has a good number of useful tools—and it’s affordable, too. While it might be bulky and heavy, we have to admit it’s a decent value. We don’t expect it to hold up to intense use, but in a “save your butt” kind of capacity, it’s certainly holds up to light use.

The long-nosed pliers, wire cutter, and wire stripper all worked reasonably well, as did the can and bottle openers and various screwdrivers. RoverTac claims the tool includes a saw blade, but it’s more like a serrated knife, which worked—just not very well.

The plain knife blade is sharper than it looks and easily cut through rope and twine during our tests. The 12-in-1 comes with a sewn nylon sheath to attach to your belt. Don’t expect this to be the pride of your tool collection, but when you need it most, it will be there.

While no multitool can replace a set of full-size hand tools, the Gerber Gear Center-Drive multitool is by far the closest that we’ve tested. The foldable center-axis provides a lot more length in comparison to the average multitool screwdriver, which gives you extra reach for tight spaces.

The blade on the Center-Drive is also the longest of any that we’ve tested. It feels large enough to take on real cutting responsibility like thick rope or small branches. The high-carbon steel also ensures long-term durability so you don’t have to worry about constantly sharpening the blade between uses.

The Center-Drive is bulkier than other options on this list, but the included nylon sheath is designed to slip onto your belt. Another plus is that there’s a full bit set included.

Fresh out of the box, the Swiss Tool Spirit X impressed us with its design and finish. The tools are packed into the frame very closely, like scientific instrumentation. All the tools—save one—deploy from the outside of the frame, so you can access them without much hassle. The company claims 24 tools in this multitool, but we counted 23, including one that’s simply a hook for a lanyard.

While the needle-nose pliers, wire cutters, scissors, three standard screwdrivers, and can opener work well, it was the less common tools that really impressed us. This is the first multi we’ve seen with a metal saw, which is on the edge of the file. It cut through mild steel hardware surprisingly well, and the file did a nice job cleaning up the edges when we were done.

The Phillips screwdriver shank flares out at the end so that all four points on the head are the same size, making for very solid engagement. The Spirit X’s bottle opener is made from wide stainless steel stock, which keeps it flat on the bottle cap so it doesn’t slip or cut into the cap. The combination reamer-punch efficiently opens up holes in wood, leather, and soft metals, and it can drill holes through 3⁄4-inch pine board.

An all-around great pick, this multitool will get the job done, no matter what that job happens to be.

Full Victorinox Swiss Tool Spirit X Multitool Review

The next iteration in one of Leatherman’s most popular lines comes with a weighty price tag. But it’s justified, since we had a hard time finding fault with the Wave Alpha.

The multitool comes with a standard knife blade, a saw, a file, and a pair of scissors. The file worked well smoothing out nails, and the saw comfortably powered through small branches.

However, we were most pleasantly impressed with the scissors. They’re much larger than any other pair of scissors we've seen on a multitool (“the largest cutting surface ever on a pliers-based Leatherman,” according to the brand). Because of their size and the spring that pushes the handle back up after every snip, we were able to hold the bottom still in hand and easily use our thumb to press down on the blade to cut. This simplified cutting through large pieces of paper, even for those of us who are lefties (since nearly no scissors are designed for cutting with our dominant hand).

The classic pocket knife is made of MagnaCut steel, which is corrosion-resistant and has great edge retention. During testing, we focused on everyday items like twine, paper, cardboard, and zip ties and opening sealed packages. We never needed more than one stern pull of the blade to get through any of them.

The central tool of the Wave Alpha is the plier-wire cutter, which we found easy to use thanks to the biting grip of the ridges and the ergonomic handle.

Though Leatherman lists 16 tools, we counted closer to 12. For instance, the file is designated as two separate tools, with the traditional flat side counting as one and the diamond-coated edge counting as another. That’s a fairly common embellishment with multitool descriptions.

Full Leatherman Wave Alpha Multitool Review

With its svelte, minimalist frame featuring three main tools, this Gerber cuts down on the unnecessary junk and keeps its tools simple and effective.

As a pocket knife–based multitool, it features a full 3-inch, locking plain blade. Although it isn’t the sharpest right out of the box, it cut cleanly through paper, plastic, rope, twine, and steak, and was adequate for some light whittling.

The side opposite the blade features a hex bit driver and scissors. The driver has a reversible bit in a magnetic holder—we love this because you get legit flat and Phillips screwdrivers that just plain work.

The scissors are a bit larger than those found on other models and were easy to control when cutting out intricate shapes from paper to medium cardboard. Between the scissors and the driver is a sharp, narrow awl. We weren't able to use this to drill holes in wood and plastic, but it works well, as intended, to poke holes through leather and canvas.

Rounding out the eight functions is a nice bottle opener that pivots off the end of the tool frame. It doubles as a pry bar (the bottle opener flipped over) and a “hammer” (the wide base of the bottle opener). Is it less a hammer and more just a flat surface for hitting things? Sure. But when you need to finish tapping in a tent stake or small nail, it’ll do.

The plier-based Leatherman Signal comes with several standard items, including a stainless steel blade and a serrated saw. However, it impressed us most with its several outdoor-specific functions.

These include a detachable ferro rod that, in combination with the serrated saw, creates sparks for your campfire. The ferro rod also doubles as an emergency whistle. During testing, I was particularly pleased with the carabiner on the bottom of the multitool. While not a major feature, being able to clip it onto my hiking backpack and forget about it made it so much easier to carry with me than other options.

Perhaps the only major downside is the hammer tool. It functions more like a blunt, flat end you can use in a pinch.

Everyday life doesn’t always require a saw, hammer, or bulky pliers. The Leatherman Micra is a keychain tool, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything else. The Micra hosts a number of items that are still quite handy when small and, importantly, are often the most useful in day-to-day life.

The multitool is built around a pair of scissors, which are the perfect size for cutting tags and snipping loose threads. Tools on the body include tweezers, a nail file and cleaner, a small screwdriver, and a bottle opener, among others.

While carrying the Leatherman Micra around, I was genuinely astonished at how often I used it. I frequently pulled it out for small tasks like picking something out from under my nails, plucking a small hair out of place, or tightening the screws on my sunglasses’ hinges.

The Micra works so well because it knows what it is. The convenience and portability make it hard to go anywhere without it.

With its wide frame and large plier jaws, the Dual-Force is a beast of a multitool. You can open the pliers and slip the pivot to spread the dual-position jaws extra wide to grab large fasteners or objects. The jaws feature three separate gripping areas: two for large or small round objects and one for gripping flat things. We appreciated their versatility for holding well in a variety of situations.

One of our favorite things about the Dual-Force is that all the other tools are accessible when the pliers are closed. This multitool also features a bit holder with two Phillips and one plain screwdriver bit. We regard these among the most useful multitool screwdrivers available, although they are sometimes difficult to use in tight spaces.

The Dual-Force is rounded out with a large knife, a saw blade, and a three-sided file. The knife blade is reasonably sharp out of the box, and we easily cut through thick rope with it. We used the saw blade to cut both green and dried-out sticks and branches with relative ease. We were able to use the file on both wood and metal, although it was better suited for the metal.

While the number of tools and functionalities on your multitool isn’t the only measure of how helpful it’ll be, it does give you a sense of its versatility. The multitools we recommend have anywhere from five to 20 or more different functions.

Note that, in their descriptions, manufacturers often count different capabilities of a specific tool individually to arrive at a higher number of “tools.” Pliers, for example, may be counted three or four times if they can function as needle-nose pliers, regular pliers, wire cutters, and wire strippers.

It’s key to pay attention to the quality of each tool and, of course, how often you’ll use them. For instance, a multitool with a screwdriver attachment is great, but if that multitool’s grip doesn’t give you the leverage to twist off seized screws or only comes with one screwdriver bit, it’s far less effective in practice.

We recommend starting your search by listing three or four tools you use most. Then, opt for a multitool that performs well at those functions. A multitool that has a few tools you use frequently will end up being more valuable to you than one packed to the brim with tools you don’t use much at all.

One of the key reasons to own a multitool is for its portability and convenience compared with carrying a full set of tools. So, if you can’t fit it in a pocket or in the center console of your car, it’s probably too big. That said, size isn’t everything. Each item on a multitool needs enough space from the others to work effectively, and you need to make sure you have a good grip for leverage.

The weight of a multitool only becomes a problem if it is too heavy to comfortably clip onto a belt or slip into a pocket. The majority of the tools on our list are made of stainless steel, which is durable yet relatively lightweight.

Can a Multitool Replace a Tool Kit? In short, no. Multitools are useful in a pinch or when you just need them for a quick fix, but they cannot replace a full tool kit. The biggest utility of a multitool is its convenience. It can function well enough for small repairs or to get by when you’ve got nothing else nearby.

We designed our tests to utilize every tool and function of each model. We carved white pine boards and maple branches. We opened bottles, cans, and shipping packaging. We disassembled and reassembled an old British carburetor, an electrical junction box, and a standard three-prong outlet.

We cut rope, twine, lamp wire, 14-gauge indoor branch circuit wire, maple saplings, branches, paper, and plastic. We also stripped the wires we cut and crimped electrical connectors. With the pliers, we gripped, squeezed, twisted, and turned various bits of hardware. Finally, we filed wood, metal, and even our own fingernails.

During these tests, we paid close attention to the performance of the tool in the given task, the ease of use, how each multitool ergonomically fit in our hand as we worked, and how we expect each tool to last over a long period of time. After all that was said and done, we noted our impressions to compile our final list.

For testing across the board, we evaluated each tool in common situations. For instance, the saw isn’t likely going to cut through 2x4s, so we opted for small branches, twine, and cardboard boxes.

Tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling. He began his career as an intern at Popular Mechanics, then worked as an editor at Outside, spearheading the magazine's gear coverage and biannual Buyer's Guide. Now that he's back, he leads product reviews for PopMech, as well as Runner's World, Best Products, and Biography. #6410. This Dietary Supplement Could Have Potential Brain Benefits, Study Finds

A supplement containing a substance naturally made by gut bacteria increased blood flow to a memory-related brain region in adults with obesity, raising new questions about its potential benefits.

When the brain works harder, it needs more blood to supply oxygen and nutrients. For people with obesity, changes in blood vessel function can affect circulation, raising questions about how well the brain responds to these demands. A new clinical trial suggests a dietary supplement could help increase blood flow during mental activity, although researchers have yet to show that it improves memory.

Researchers at the University of Oklahoma investigated urolithin A, a substance produced when certain gut bacteria break down compounds found in foods such as strawberries, pomegranates, and walnuts. The amount people naturally produce varies, and existing research suggests that production declines with age and increasing body mass index. Urolithin A is also available as a dietary supplement.

In the randomized clinical trial, published in JAMA Network Open, 50 adults with obesity, ages 40 to 64, received either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A daily or a placebo for four weeks.

Participants taking the supplement showed a greater increase in blood flow to the brain while completing a challenging memory task. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area involved in holding and using information over short periods. However, researchers found no significant improvements in blood vessel function in the arm or performance on memory tests.

“The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity,” said first author Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health.”

According to the researchers, this is the first human study to report an effect of urolithin A on blood vessel function in the brain. The supplement was well-tolerated, although the trial involved relatively few participants at a single research site. Longer studies with larger groups will be needed to determine whether the changes in blood flow lead to lasting health benefits.

“These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain,” said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. “Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits.”

The researchers ultimately hope to find ways to help people maintain their cognitive health as they age.

“The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline,” Langley said. “We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives.”

Reference: “Urolithin A and Endothelial and Cerebrovascular Function in Middle-Aged Adults With Obesity: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi-Langley, Rafal Gulej, Zalan Kaposzta, Zsofia Szarvas, Ali Shahriari, Henry Kinnard, Bryan Ticer, Camila B. Pinto, Peter Mukli, Mihaly Muranyi, Cheryl Adams, Jeng Kong, Leah Anderson, Stefano Tarantini, Yan Daniel Zhao, Norman G. Hord and Andriy Yabluchanskiy, 9 October 2026, JAMA Network Open. DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38047

Research reported in this publication was supported by the American Heart Association (grant No. 24DIVSUP1282484 awarded to Dr da Costa Pinaffi-Langley) and the Reynolds Foundation.

#6409. A paleontologist hiking near Arches National Park may have found a new armored dinosaur

A new dinosaur bonebed discovered near Moab, Utah, may contain an unknown armored dinosaur species dating back 138 to 141 million years.

In mid-October 2026, the Utah Geological Survey (UGS) opened a new dinosaur excavation near Moab, in eastern Utah. The team calls the site the Ironstone Bonebed, and it lies north of Arches National Park.

The bonebed appears to contain the remains of a new species of armored dinosaur, the agency said. State Paleontologist Jim Kirkland is describing the animal and naming it in honor of Don DeBlieux, the Utah assistant state paleontologist.

The site is estimated at 138 million to 141 million years old. The UGS called it “currently tied as potentially the oldest Cretaceous dinosaur bonebed in North America.”

DeBlieux has said he spotted the first fossils while exploring the area on foot. They were a shoulder blade and an upper arm bone from an armored dinosaur.

He oversees the UGS field paleontology program and its fossil preparation lab. In 2002, he found a skull weathering out of sandstone near the middle of the Wahweap Formation, in southern Utah’s Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

That skull became the horned dinosaur Diabloceratops eatoni. DeBlieux spent more than 800 hours over two years removing the rock from around the bone.

Kirkland has said the crew has identified about four kinds of dinosaurs at the new site so far.

Kirkland, who has held his post since 1999, is known for naming numerous dinosaur species, most notably Utahraptor. After 25 years of working side by side with him, DeBlieux will retire at the end of 2026.

Geologically, the new locality is nearly equivalent to Doelling’s Bowl, a UGS site some six miles (10 kilometers) to the east.

DeBlieux also found Doelling’s Bowl, in 2005, when he came across the vertebrae and a hip bone of a dromaeosaurid, a raptor-like predator.

A 2012 study of Utah raptors named it Yurgovuchia doellingi and reported a bone bed covering tens of acres (at least several hectares).

Plant-eating iguanodonts, including one compared to Iguanacolossus, dominate it, with at least ten individuals. At least three polacanthine ankylosaurs, a group of armored dinosaurs, were also found there.

The bonebed lies in the lower Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation, below a marker layer of calcrete. It yielded Mierasaurus bobyoungi, a long-necked sauropod descended from Jurassic turiasaurs of the Iberian Peninsula.

Kirkland and DeBlieux co-authored its 2017 description. By then, Doelling’s Bowl had also produced teeth from a large allosauroid predator and a new, still unnamed species of polacanthid ankylosaur.

“Ankylosaurs were so well protected that even their eyelids were armored,” Kirkland and Mark Loewen, then of the Utah Museum of Natural History, wrote in 2011.

At the time, the Cedar Mountain Formation had yielded more ankylosaur species than any other geologic formation in the world. Several more from it had been found but not yet described.

Gastonia burgei came from the basal Yellow Cat Member. It was closely related to Polacanthus foxi, from nearly age-equivalent rocks on England’s Isle of Wight.

Younger layers have produced other Cedar Mountain dinosaurs, including the ankylosaur Peloroplites cedrimontanus from the Ruby Ranch Member.

Utah’s first known nodosaurid, Animantarx ramaljonesi, was the first dinosaur discovered solely by technology. A radiological technician found it in 1994 by mapping low-level radiation across a quarry near the top of the formation.

Cedarpelta bilbyhallorum was then North America’s only known ankylosaurid from the Lower Cretaceous. Ankylosaurids are the branch of armored dinosaurs known for tail clubs and boxy skulls.

The UGS expects the new site to shed light on the transition from the Jurassic to the Cretaceous. A catastrophic event at the end of the Jurassic led to the near-complete extinction of Utah’s Morrison Formation dinosaurs, including Stegosaurus.

Across most of the western North American mountain belt, the gap between Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks spans 20 million to 25 million years.

In eastern Utah, microfossils, chemical signatures and uranium-lead dating of ancient soils cut it to five million to seven million years.

Kirkland, DeBlieux and two colleagues reported that revised dating in a 2025 conference abstract. In those rocks, an increase in larger coelurosaurs, a group of meat-eating dinosaurs, documents the extinction.

The ancient soils also point to a short wet interval after the drier Late Jurassic. Where Early Cretaceous wetlands formed in eastern Utah appears to have been controlled by movement of ancient salt deposits.

Kirkland has argued that the same salt tectonics explain why Utah’s oldest Cretaceous dinosaurs are restricted to northern Grand County.

As buried salt beds were squeezed into ridges, nearby ground subsided, and Lower Cretaceous sediments collected in the low areas.

Across much of the rest of North America, erosion was removing rock at the time. Salt movement peaked in the early Mesozoic, as reflected by the Salt Valley anticline at Arches National Park and the Moab fault.

The information was obtained from the Utah Geological Survey.

Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold bear would have been worn on a headdress.

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan have discovered a unique gold bear figurine in a 2,200-year-old burial mound that looters had hit but failed to empty completely.

The sculpted bear stands on its hind limbs and holds a pot-like container between its front paws. The artifact would have been worn as part of a headdress, and holes at its base indicate that it could have been sewn onto the garment, according to a translated statement from the Kazakhstan government.

The 2,200-year-old gold bear is a unique find in Kazakhstan.

The gold bear was unearthed at an Early Iron Age burial mound at the Karagaily burial ground in the southern city of Almaty, along with a surprisingly high number of human bones for a single burial mound.

Although other gold-crafted animals have been found in the region, the newly unearthed bear is the first of its kind.

"The sculpted bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered previously," Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museums Association, which conducted the excavation, said in the statement. "This discovery allows us to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to Altai."

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan excavated a 2,200-year-old burial mound.

The figurine dates to the Saka period, named for a nomadic horseback-riding people from Iran who lived on the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin of what is now western China. Archaeologists have found comparable gold objects at other excavations in Kazakhstan, according to the statement. For example, a headdress element shaped like a small leopard previously came to light at the Almaty Kok-Kainar burial ground, which dates to the fourth century B.C. Also, the headdress of Kazakhstan's famous "Golden Man," a young Iron Age warrior buried in an extraordinarily lavish grave, also has a gold, sheep-shaped decorative element.

It's unclear which bear species the figurine depicts, but today Kazakhstan is home to two subspecies of brown bear: the Tien Shan or Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), which lives in the Tien Shan Mountains in the southeast, and the East Siberian brown bear (Ursus arctos collaris) in the Altai Mountains in the east, according to a study published earlier this year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Preliminary analyses date the recently excavated site to the fourth to third centuries B.C., according to the statement. Based on the number of bones they excavated, experts suspect that the mound, which is around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and roughly 85 feet (26 m) wide, may have been the final resting place for four adults and three children.

Archaeologists found a surprising number of human bones in the burial mound.

"Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single burial mound, as such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan," Marat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior research fellow at the Almaty Museums Association, said in the statement. "As a rule, burial mounds of a comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people."

Archaeologists also found pieces of Saka pottery, most of which had been strewn about after the burial had been looted in ancient times, according to the statement. The thieves left behind a 10-foot (3 m) looting pit.

"Research into the Karagaily burial ground is ongoing," Nurpeisov said in the statement. "To clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals interred, further analyses are planned, including the involvement of anthropologists."

After all of the investigations are finished, some of the artifacts will be put on display at the Almaty Museum, according to the statement.
